name: Bias Audits, Accessibility Checks, and Incident Reports
title: Bias Audits, Accessibility Checks, and Incident Reports
answer: Bias audits, accessibility checks, and incident reports are three routine reviews that keep AI tools honest as a school's use of them grows. They matter because a tool can look fair on paper yet still treat groups of students differently, shut out students with disabilities, or fail quietly without anyone tracking it. Together they turn one-time approval into ongoing oversight.

crumbs.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule

sections.body: This idea sets out three recurring checks that a school runs after an AI tool is in use, not just when it is bought. A bias check asks whether the tool treats groups of students differently, and it looks at who actually gets flagged, placed, or disciplined rather than trusting that balanced data produced fair results. An accessibility check asks whether a tool students are required to use works with screen readers, captions, and keyboard navigation, and whether it meets the federal standard the book describes earlier. An incident report gives staff and students a simple way to flag errors, bias, or harm, with a shared form reviewed monthly and fixes published. The problem it solves is drift: a tool that passed review can still go wrong over time, and these three checks are how a school notices.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, the bias check means comparing who gets flagged, placed, or disciplined before and after a tool arrives, so the review is about outcomes rather than intentions. The accessibility check sits inside the approval review, where the technology director can ask vendors for an accessibility report, and any tool that shuts out a student with a disability is treated as not ready even if it works well for others. The incident report starts small, with a shared form that someone reads monthly and a district that publishes what it fixed, and over time those reports become the district's best evidence about which tools should stay. Students can take part in all three, and a small student advisory group meeting each quarter with school leaders will catch problems adults miss. The text does not give separate grade band versions of these checks.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with research support. It cites Li et al., 2026, whose work on test score prediction found that including balanced groups in the data did not by itself guarantee fair predictions, which is why the bias check has to examine results and not only inputs. It also cites Moore et al., 2026, a two year project in which an advisory board of former students and experts helped improve a high school AI curriculum, with student learning gains larger in the second year. The accessibility check is tied to the federal standard described earlier in the book rather than to a separate study.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are built into how the checks are run. A bias check that only inspects inputs will miss unfair results, so the comparison of who is flagged, placed, or disciplined is the part that matters. An accessibility check is a gate, and a tool that excludes a student with a disability is not ready no matter how good it is for everyone else. An incident report only works if someone actually reads it and the district publishes what it fixed, so the form alone is not the safeguard. The decisions stay with people: staff and students raise the reports, the technology director asks vendors for accessibility reports, and school leaders review the findings and decide which tools remain on the list.
